relevance_reason: Reports two sisters with a homozygous WASHC4 variant causing MRT43, which expands the phenotype to include skeletal muscle involvement, together with functional studies.

findings.statement: Gangfuß et al. (2022) reported 2 sisters with a syndromic phenotype that included dysmorphic features, intellectual disability, profound developmental disorder, and skeletal muscle involvement. The authors said these features expanded the clinical spectrum of WASHC4-related disease, and they compared the phenotype with previously reported cases.
quotes: Homozygous WASHC4 variant in two sisters causes a syndromic phenotype defined by dysmorphisms, intellectual disability, profound developmental disorder, and skeletal muscle involvement.
Here, we report two siblings with a homozygous WASHC4 variant expanding the clinical spectrum of the disease and provide a phenotypical comparison with cases reported in the literature.

findings.statement: In 2 sisters with intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, and skeletal muscle involvement, Gangfuß et al. (2022) identified a homozygous variant in the WASHC4 gene. The abstract does not give the specific variant.
quotes: Here, we report two siblings with a homozygous WASHC4 variant expanding the clinical spectrum of the disease

findings.statement: Gangfuß et al. (2022) found that proteomic profiling of fibroblasts from a WASHC4-deficient patient showed dysregulation of proteins relevant for maintaining the neuromuscular axis. Immunostaining of the same patient's muscle biopsy confirmed dysregulation of proteins needed for proper muscle function. The authors said histologic studies and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering microscopy supported a role for WASHC4 in protein processing and clearance in humans.
quotes: Proteomic profiling of fibroblasts of the WASHC4-deficient patient revealed dysregulation of proteins relevant for the maintenance of the neuromuscular axis.

Immunostaining on a muscle biopsy derived from the same patient confirmed dysregulation of proteins relevant for proper muscle function, thus highlighting an affliction of muscle cells upon loss of functional WASHC4.

The results of histological and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering microscopic studies support the concept of a functional role of the WASHC4 protein in humans by altering protein processing and clearance.

relevance_reason: The paper reports a retrospective clinical re-analysis of the seven Omani children homozygous for WASHC4 c.3056C>G (p.Pro1019Arg) that defines MRT43, documents newly recognized motor features, and provides functional and mouse-model evidence that this variant destabilizes the WASH complex and causes endo-lysosomal dysfunction with cognitive and motor impairments.

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from 7 children with homozygous WASHC4 c.3056C>G mutations originally reported by Ropers et al. (2011), who had been evaluated at the Royal Hospital, Muscat, Oman. Although developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary reason for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms at a mean age of 10.4 years, with movements described as 'clumsy' and with fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical exam.
quotes: We retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from seven children with homozygous WASHC4c.3056C>G mutations (obtained by Dr. Rajab in 2010 at the Royal Hospital, Muscat, Oman).

While developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary impetus for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms (mean age=10.4 years old, Figure 8H). The patients’ movements were described as ‘clumsy’ with notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical exam (Figure 8H).
(H) Table of motor findings in clinical exam of human patients with the homozygous SWIPP1019R mutation. All patients exhibit motor dysfunction (+ = symptom present).

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) reported that recent communication with the parents of the WASHC4 c.3056C>G homozygous patients, who were by then an average of 21 years old, revealed no notable exacerbation of symptoms; the authors suggested that the SWIPP1019R mouse model either differs from human patients or may predict future disease progression in these individuals, since mice worsened significantly at 5-6 months of age (thought to be equivalent to ~30-35 human years).
quotes: Recent communication with the parents of these patients, who are now an average of 21 years old, revealed no notable symptom exacerbation. It is therefore possible that the SWIPP1019R mouse model either exhibits differences from human patients or may predict future disease progression for these individuals, given that we observed significant worsening at 5–6 months old in mice (which is thought to be equivalent to ~30–35 years old in humans)

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) studied the autosomal recessive WASHC4 mutation c.3056C>G (p.Pro1019Arg), previously identified by Ropers et al. (2011) in a cohort of children with nonsyndromic intellectual disability, noting that the affected residue lies in a region of SWIP thought to be critical for binding the WASH component Strumpellin. Co-immunoprecipitation in HEK cells showed that mutant SWIP pulled down significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wild-type SWIP (54.8% and 41.4% of wild type, respectively), indicating that the mutation hinders WASH complex formation.
quotes: an autosomal recessive mutation in WASHC4 (c.3056C>G; p.Pro1019Arg) was identified in a cohort of children with non-syndromic intellectual disability (Ropers et al., 2011)

This C>G point mutation results in a Proline>Arginine substitution at position 1019 of SWIP’s amino acid sequence (Figure 2A), a region thought to be critical for its binding to the WASH component, Strumpellin

Compared to WT, MUT SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 (IP: 54.8% and 41.4% of WT SWIP, respectively), suggesting that the SWIPP1019R mutation hinders WASH complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) proposed that WASH complex destabilization resulting from SWIPP1019R drives cognitive and motor impairments via endo-lysosomal dysfunction in the brain, with accumulation of neurodegenerative markers including upregulation of unfolded protein response modulators and lysosomal enzymes, lipofuscin build-up, and cleaved caspase-3 over time.
quotes: Combined, these findings support the model that WASH complex destabilization, resulting from SWIPP1019R, drives cognitive and motor impairments via endo-lysosomal dysfunction in the brain.

the data presented here support a mechanistic model whereby SWIPP1019R causes a loss of WASH complex function, resulting in endo-lysosomal disruption and accumulation of neurodegenerative markers, such as upregulation of unfolded protein response modulators and lysosomal enzymes, as well as build-up of lipofuscin and cleaved caspase-3 over time.

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) generated a CRISPR knock-in mouse carrying a CCT>CGT point mutation in exon 29 of murine Washc4, mimicking the human WASHC4 c.3056C>G (SWIPP1019R) variant. Western blotting of adult whole-brain lysate from homozygous mutant mice showed near-complete loss of the WASH complex members Strumpellin (3.8% of wild type) and WASH1 (1.1% of wild type), phenocopying data from the human patients and indicating WASH complex instability in vivo.
quotes: A CRISPR-induced CCT>CGT point mutation was introduced into exon 29 of Washc4.
Strumpellin (WT 100.0±5.1%, MUT 3.8±0.9%, t2.14=18.60, p=0.0021) and WASH1 (WT 100.0±4.3%, MUT 1.1±0.4%, t2.1=22.77, p=0.0018) were significantly decreased.
These results phenocopied data from the human patients (Ropers et al., 2011) and suggested that the WASH complex is unstable in the presence of this SWIP point mutation in vivo.

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) found by tandem-mass-tag spatial proteomics of 10-month-old SWIPP1019R mutant mouse brain that four WASH proteins (WASHC1, WASHC2, WASHC4, WASHC5) and RAB21A were differentially abundant in all seven subcellular fractions, that 728 proteins differed overall between genotypes, and that a WASH/CCC/Retriever/CORVET-HOPS-containing endosomal module (M38) was significantly decreased while a lysosomal module (M36) containing cathepsins, hydrolases and progranulin was significantly increased in mutant brain.
quotes: Five proteins were differentially abundant between WT and MUT in all seven fractions, including four WASH proteins (WASHC1, WASHC2, WASHC4, WASHC5) and RAB21A – a known WASH interactor that functions in early endosomal trafficking
At this level, there were 728 differentially abundant proteins between WT and MUT brain (Benjamini–Hochberg FDR<0.05)
In contrast to the decreased abundance of the WASH complex/endosome module (M38), M36 exhibited increased abundance in MUT brain (Figure 4C).

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) showed that cultured cortical neurons from SWIPP1019R homozygous mutant mice had enlarged somatic EEA1+ early endosomes without a change in puncta number, and fewer but larger Cathepsin D+ lysosomal puncta than wild-type neurons, consistent with a loss-of-function mutation producing morphological abnormalities of the endo-lysosomal pathway.
quotes: Reconstructed three-dimensional volumes of EEA1 and Cathepsin D puncta revealed that MUT neurons display larger EEA1+ somatic puncta than WT neurons (Figure 5G and J), but no difference in the total number of EEA1+ puncta (Figure 5F).
Conversely, MUT neurons exhibited significantly less Cathepsin D+ puncta than WT neurons (Figure 5H), but the remaining puncta were significantly larger than those of WT neurons (Figure 5I and K).

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) found that 10-month-old SWIPP1019R mutant mice had significantly increased cleaved caspase-3 staining in motor cortex (44.0% vs 25.4% of DAPI+ nuclei) but not at adolescence, and that transmission electron microscopy of 7-month-old mutant motor cortex revealed large electron-dense lipofuscin deposits; dopaminergic cell number in substantia nigra pars compacta and striatal dopaminergic innervation were unchanged, suggesting motor cortex was the primary movement-related region altered.
quotes: No difference is seen at P42, but the amount of CC3+ nuclei is significantly higher in aged MUT mice (P42 WT 6.97 ± 0.80%, P42 MUT 5.26 ± 0.90%, 10mo WT 25.38 ± 2.05%, 10mo MUT 44.01 ± 1.90%, H=74.12, p<0.0001).
Strikingly, we observed large electron-dense inclusions in the cell bodies of MUT neurons (arrows, Figure 6L; pseudo-colored region, 6N).

Consistent with these findings, there were no significant differences in dopaminergic cell number in the substantia nigra pars compacta or in dopaminergic innervation of the striatum in adult brain, suggesting that the motor cortex was the primary movement-related region altered in SWIPP109R brain

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) reported that SWIPP1019R homozygous mutant mice performed normally in novel object recognition and Y-maze alternation but showed a significant deficit in cued fear memory recall 48 hours after tone-footshock pairing at both adolescence (P42) and adulthood (6.5 months), with intact responses to footshock and tones, consistent with the hypothesis that SWIPP1019R causes cognitive impairment in humans.
quotes: Interestingly, MUT mice performed equivalently to WT mice in episodic and working memory paradigms, including novel object recognition and Y-maze alternations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). However, in a fear conditioning task, MUT mice displayed a significant deficit in cued fear memory (Figure 7).

These data demonstrate that although MUT mice perceive footshock sensations and auditory cues, it is their memory of these paired events that is significantly impaired. Additionally, this deficit in fear response was evident at both adolescence and adulthood
These changes are consistent with the hypothesis that SWIPP109R is the cause of cognitive impairments in humans.

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) found that SWIPP1019R homozygous mutant mice showed an almost 50% reduction in rotarod retention time at both P45 and 5.5 months, and that TreadScan gait analysis, largely normal at adolescence, revealed by 5.5 months significantly longer hindlimb swing times, longer stride lengths, and decreased homologous coupling, demonstrating progressive motor decline.
quotes: At both ages, the MUT mice exhibited an almost 50% reduction in their ability to remain on the rod (top, P45: WT 169.9 ± 25.7 s, MUT 83.8 ± 15.9 s, U=35, p=0.0054; bottom, 5.5mo: WT 135.9 ± 20.9 s, MUT 66.7 ± 9.5 s, t18=3.011, p=0.0075).
At 5.5mo (bottom), MUT mice display significantly longer rear swing time (WT 140 ± 6.2 ms, MUT 252.0 ± 21.6 ms, t12=4.988, p=0.0003).

These findings demonstrate that SWIPP1019R results in progressive motor function decline that was detectable by the rotarod task at adolescence, but which became more prominent with age, as both gait and strength functions deteriorated.

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) used in vivo BioID with a WASH1-BioID2 probe expressed under the human synapsin-1 promoter in mouse brain to define the neuronal WASH complex proteome, identifying 175 significantly enriched proteins (fold-change >=4, FDR <0.05) that included all five WASH complex subunits and 13 previously reported WASH interactors, as well as endosomal, endocytic, cytoskeletal and excitatory postsynaptic proteins, supporting a major endosomal trafficking role for WASH in mouse brain.
quotes: The resulting neuronal WASH proteome included 175 proteins that were significantly enriched (fold-change≥4.0, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR<0.05, Figure 1G; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). Of these proteins, we identified all five WASH complex components (Figure 1H), as well as 13 previously reported WASH complex interactors
Taken together, these results support a major endosomal trafficking role of the WASH complex in mouse brain.

findings.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) noted that dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8), and that autosomal recessive point mutations in WASHC4 (SWIP) and WASHC5 are associated with syndromic and nonsyndromic intellectual disabilities.
quotes: dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (protein: Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8) (de Bot et al., 2013; Valdmanis et al., 2007), and autosomal recessive point mutations in WASHC4 (protein: SWIP) and WASHC5 are associated with syndromic and non-syndromic intellectual disabilities (Assoum et al., 2020; Elliott et al., 2013; Ropers et al., 2011)

relevance_reason: Reports three new patients from two families with compound heterozygous KIAA1033/WASHC4 variants causing syndromic ARID (MRT43).

findings.statement: Assoum et al. (2020) described 2 sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, with syndromic intellectual disability. Both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules. The younger sister also had congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
quotes: Two sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, had a stop-gain and a missense variants
Both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules.
In addition, the younger sibling had a congenital absence of the right internal carotid and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

phenotypes.text: congenital absence of right internal carotid artery

findings.statement: In 2 sisters with syndromic intellectual disability, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous variants in the KIAA1033 (WASHC4) gene by exome sequencing: a stop-gain variant (p.Gln442Ter) and a missense variant (p.Asp1048Gly), each inherited from one parent.
quotes: Here we describe three additional patients (from two unrelated families) with syndromic ID due to compound heterozygous KIAA1033 variants ascertained by exome sequencing (ES).
Two sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, had a stop-gain and a missense variants, each inherited from one parent (p.(Gln442*) and p.(Asp1048Gly)).

findings.statement: Assoum et al. (2020) described a 34-year-old patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly.
quotes: The third patient was aged 34 years and had two missense variants
This patient presented with mild ID, short stature, and microcephaly.

findings.statement: In a 34-year-old patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous missense variants in the KIAA1033 gene, p.Lys1079Arg and p.His503Arg, one inherited from each parent, by exome sequencing.
quotes: The third patient was aged 34 years and had two missense variants, one inherited from each parent (p.(Lys1079Arg) and p.(His503Arg)).

findings.statement: Assoum et al. (2020) concluded that KIAA1033 is responsible for a heterogeneous autosomal recessive intellectual disability phenotype and that further descriptions would be needed to refine the clinical phenotype.
quotes: We conclude that KIAA1033 is responsible for a heterogeneous ARID phenotype, and additional description will be needed to refine the clinical phenotype.

relevance_reason: Reports the identification of a SWIP mutation in a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability, the defining report for MRT43.

findings.statement: Ropers et al. (2011) studied a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID), which they described as non-syndromic.
quotes: In a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID)
Identification of a novel candidate gene for non-syndromic autosomal recessive intellectual disability

findings.statement: In a large consanguineous family with ARID, Ropers et al. (2011) used homozygosity mapping, together with targeted exon enrichment and high-throughput sequencing, to identify the underlying gene defect.
quotes: we have combined homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment and high-throughput sequencing to identify the underlying gene defect

findings.statement: In affected members of a large consanguineous family with ARID, Ropers et al. (2011) found a non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP gene, a member of the WASH complex. After SNP filtering, it was one of only two remaining changes. The authors considered it causative based on high pathogenicity and evolutionary conservation scores and on functional considerations. Functional studies showed that the mutation significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex.
quotes: After appropriate single-nucleotide polymorphism filtering, only two molecular changes remained, including a non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP [Strumpellin and WASH (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and scar homolog)-interacting protein] gene
Based on high pathogenicity and evolutionary conservation scores as well as functional considerations, this gene defect was considered as causative for ID in this family.
we could show that this mutation leads to significantly reduced SWIP levels and to destabilization of the entire WASH complex

variants.as_reported: non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP gene

findings.statement: Ropers et al. (2011) noted that SWIP belongs to the WASH complex, which is involved in actin polymerization and in multiple endosomal transport processes. They suggested that SWIP is a novel gene for ARID, because the mutation destabilized the WASH complex.
quotes: a member of the recently discovered WASH complex, which is involved in actin polymerization and multiple endosomal transport processes
Thus, our findings suggest that SWIP is a novel gene for ARID.
